explanations.explanation: The LORD tells Moses, "Gather the people so that I may give them water." (Numbers 21:16) Not a committee, not a select few. The whole crowd gets the invitation, and that's a lot of folks to line up at one well. I'd hate to be the one holding the clipboard.

The elders are good guesses, since leaders show up all over the Bible. But the LORD's words to Moses at Beer are "Gather the people so that I may give them water." (Numbers 21:16) So it's the whole people, not just a few leaders. Everybody gets a seat at this table.

Priests are a fair guess, friend, but they aren't mentioned in this verse at all. The LORD says to Moses, "Gather the people so that I may give them water." (Numbers 21:16) That means everybody, from the front of the line to the back. Nobody gets left out of this one.

Water it is. The LORD says, "Gather the people so that I may give them water." (Numbers 21:16) Out in the wilderness, a well is a big deal. I once got excited about a single crumb of dough, so I get it.

Bread makes sense, because people in the wilderness always need to eat. But at Beer the LORD says He will give them water, not bread. The words are "Gather the people so that I may give them water." (Numbers 21:16) The clue was the well, friend. A well is a pretty big hint.

Meat is a hungry guess, and I respect it. But this verse is about a well, and the LORD says He will give them water. His words are "Gather the people so that I may give them water." (Numbers 21:16) I'd take a cookie in the wilderness myself, but the verse only talks about water.
True! "Then Israel sang this song: 'Spring up, O well, all of you sing to it!'" (Numbers 21:17) They sing right to the well. I talk to my ovens, so I'm not here to judge. Sing on, friend.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, "Then Israel sang this song: 'Spring up, O well, all of you sing to it!'" (Numbers 21:17) So Israel does sing at the well. The song even talks straight to the well. Next time, trust the music.

Yes, the song says, "The princes dug the well; the nobles of the people hollowed it out with their scepters and with their staffs." (Numbers 21:18) Princes and nobles, scepters and staffs. A scepter is something you usually hold up high, so a scepter near the dirt makes me grin. I'd love to have seen that.

The priests and Levites are good guesses, but the song doesn't mention them. It says, "The princes dug the well; the nobles of the people hollowed it out with their scepters and with their staffs." (Numbers 21:18) So the diggers are princes and nobles. Scepters, friend. SCEPTERS.

Elders and judges would make a fine digging crew, but the song gives different names. It says, "The princes dug the well; the nobles of the people hollowed it out with their scepters and with their staffs." (Numbers 21:18) Princes and nobles are the ones in the song. That's a lot of fancy hands in the dirt.

explanations.answer: Permission to pass through his land
explanations.explanation: Right. The messengers say, "Let us pass through your land." (Numbers 21:22) They're only asking to walk through. That's a polite request, like asking to cut through a parking lot, only with a whole camp behind you.

explanations.answer: A share of the water in his wells
explanations.explanation: Water is a sensible guess, but they actually promise not to touch it. They say they won't "…drink water from any well." (Numbers 21:22) What they ask for is simple: "Let us pass through your land." (Numbers 21:22)

explanations.answer: Soldiers to help them fight Moab
explanations.explanation: That would be a big ask, but it's not in the text. The messengers say only, "Let us pass through your land." (Numbers 21:22) No army, no favors, just a way through. Think of it as asking for a hallway.

True. The messengers say, "We will stay on the King’s Highway until we have passed through your territory." (Numbers 21:22) They also promise not to turn aside into any field or vineyard. That's a clear plan with no detours.

It's true, friend. The messengers say, "We will stay on the King’s Highway until we have passed through your territory." (Numbers 21:22) They also promise no turning aside into any field or vineyard, and no drinking water from any well. That is a careful promise. I once promised myself just one cookie, and we don't talk about how that went.

explanations.answer: He gathers his whole army and attacks
explanations.explanation: Yes. "…Sihon would not let Israel pass through his territory. Instead, he gathered his whole army and went out to confront Israel in the wilderness." (Numbers 21:23) Israel sent a request, and Sihon answered with an army. He came to Jahaz and fought against Israel. That's a big answer to a simple question.

explanations.answer: He lets them pass for a fee
explanations.explanation: A toll road would be a funny twist, but the text doesn't say that. Sihon "…would not let Israel pass through his territory." (Numbers 21:23) Instead he gathered his whole army and went out to meet them. There's no price tag in this story.

explanations.answer: He sends them on a longer road
explanations.explanation: A detour would be a mild answer, friend, but that's not what Sihon does. The text says he "…would not let Israel pass through his territory." (Numbers 21:23) Instead, he gathered his whole army and fought them at Jahaz. No directions, just soldiers.

Right. Israel took the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, "…but only up to the border of the Ammonites, because it was fortified." (Numbers 21:24) The text gives that one reason for the stopping point. A fortified border is a big "keep out" sign.

A flooded river is a creative guess, friend, but the text never mentions flooding. It says Israel took the land "…only up to the border of the Ammonites, because it was fortified." (Numbers 21:24) So the reason the verse gives is the fortified border. I'd read that flood story, though.

Spies do show up later in this passage, so I see where that came from. But the reason given here is different: Israel took the land "…only up to the border of the Ammonites, because it was fortified." (Numbers 21:24) The spies at Jazer come later, in verse 32.

Moab is right. Heshbon was the city of Sihon, "…who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon." (Numbers 21:26) So that land was already in Sihon's hands before Israel came along. All that history in one little verse.

Edom is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says Sihon "…had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon." (Numbers 21:26) The answer is Moab. Check the verse again and you'll only find Moab there.

Bashan comes up later, friend. That's where Og is king (Numbers 21:33). But Sihon's earlier fight was with the former king of Moab, who lost all his land as far as the Arnon (Numbers 21:26). So this one belongs to Moab.

Yes. The song says Moab's sons became refugees and "…his daughters into captivity to Sihon king of the Amorites." (Numbers 21:29) Sihon is the name in the song, and his city Heshbon is what the poets sing about. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just let it be.

Og shows up later in the chapter, so I see the mix-up. But the song says the daughters went "…into captivity to Sihon king of the Amorites." (Numbers 21:29) Og, king of Bashan, doesn't come in until verse 33. This is a heavy verse, so I'm keeping it simple.

The king of Edom isn't in this song at all. It says the daughters went "…into captivity to Sihon king of the Amorites." (Numbers 21:29) Sihon is the one named. I think this verse is a heavy one, so I'll just stick to what it says.

True, baker! "After Moses had sent spies to Jazer, Israel captured its villages and drove out the Amorites who were there." (Numbers 21:32) Scouts first, then the move. That's like checking the oven before you slide the tray in, because nobody wants to find out the hard way. The verse gives us that order.

It's true, friend. The text says, "After Moses had sent spies to Jazer, Israel captured its villages and drove out the Amorites who were there." (Numbers 21:32) So the spies go, and then Israel drives them out. That's exactly how the verse reads.

Right on the money, baker. Og and his whole army come out to meet Israel in battle at Edrei (Numbers 21:33). That's a whole army marching at them, and I think that's a moment to feel pretty small. Then the LORD says to Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand…" (Numbers 21:34) He also tells Moses to do to Og what he did to Sihon.

That sounds like a careful plan, but it's not what the LORD says. He tells Moses, "Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand…" (Numbers 21:34) No detour is given. The word is "Do not fear him…"

Messengers went to Sihon earlier (Numbers 21:21), so I see why you'd pick that. But for Og, the LORD says, "Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand…" (Numbers 21:34) This time there's no message to send. It starts with "Do not fear him…"
Land is right. The LORD says, "…I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land." (Numbers 21:34) It's people and land together. That's a big promise.

Gold would be nice, but this verse never mentions it. The LORD says, "…I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land." (Numbers 21:34) So the word is land. Nothing shiny in the list.

Cattle are a fair guess, since a king might have some. But the LORD's words are "…I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land." (Numbers 21:34) The answer is land. Cattle don't make the list.

This one is false, friend. The text says Israel struck down Og, his sons and his whole army, "…until no remnant was left. And they took possession of his land." (Numbers 21:35) So they didn't leave it behind. They took it.

False is right. "So they struck down Og, along with his sons and his whole army, until no remnant was left. And they took possession of his land." (Numbers 21:35) Israel doesn't leave Og's land behind. They take possession of it. That matches verse 34, where the LORD says He has delivered Og, his people and his land into Moses' hand.
